entries.921153820a9b22aa65ea7033a27f6c4e071e3e63: <div sID="gen9645" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Job.17" sID="Job.17"/> <div eID="gen9645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9646" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9647" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. Job reflects upon the harsh censures which his friends had passed upon him, and looking upon himself as a dying man (<reference osisRef="Job.17.1">ver. 1</reference>), he appeals to God, and begs of him speedily to appear for him, and right him, because they had wronged him, and he knew not how to right himself, <reference osisRef="Job.17.2-Job.17.7">ver. 2-7</reference>. But he hopes that, though it should be a surprise, it will be no stumbling-block, to good people, to see him thus abused, <reference osisRef="Job.17.8-Job.17.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. II. He reflects upon the vain hopes they had fed him with, that he should yet see good days, showing that his days were just at an end, and with his body all his hopes would be buried in the dust, <reference osisRef="Job.17.10-Job.17.16">ver. 10-16</reference>. His friends becoming strange to him, which greatly grieved him, he makes death and the grave familiar to him, which yielded him some comfort.
entries.1aad613159f9a63f8671ca711383ee47a9865ed4: <div eID="gen9647" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9646" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Deplorable Condition of Job; The Improvement of Job's Troubles. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9648" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My breath is corrupt, my days are extinct, the graves <hi type="italic">are ready</hi> for me. <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="italic">Are there</hi> not mockers with me? and doth not mine eye continue in their provocation? <hi type="super">3</hi> Lay down now, put me in a surety with thee; who <hi type="italic">is</hi> he <hi type="italic">that</hi> will strike hands with me? <hi type="super">4</hi> For thou hast hid their heart from understanding: therefore shalt thou not exalt <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> He that speaketh flattery to <hi type="italic">his</hi> friends, even the eyes of his children shall fail. 6 He hath made me also a byword of the people; and aforetime I was as a tabret. <hi type="super">7</hi> Mine eye also is dim by reason of sorrow, and all my members <hi type="italic">are</hi> as a shadow. <hi type="super">8</hi> Upright <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall be astonied at this, and the innocent shall stir up himself against the hypocrite. <hi type="super">9</hi> The righteous also shall hold on his way, and he that hath clean hands shall be stronger and stronger. <div eID="gen9648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9649" type="x-p"/> Job's discourse is here somewhat broken and interrupted, and he passes suddenly from one thing to another, as is usual with men in trouble; but we may reduce what is here said to three heads:— <div eID="gen9649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9650" type="x-p"/> I. The deplorable condition which poor Job was now in, which he describes, to aggravate the great unkindness of his friends to him and to justify his own complaints. Let us see what his case was. <div eID="gen9650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9651" type="x-p"/> 1. He was a dying man, <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">v. 1</reference>. He had said (<reference osisRef="Job.16.22">ch. xvi. 22</reference>), "<hi type="italic">When a few years have come,</hi> I shall go that long journey." But here he corrects himself. "Why do I talk of years to come? Alas! I am just setting out on that journey, am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. <hi type="italic">My breath is already corrupt,</hi> or broken off; my spirits are spent; I am a gone man." It is good for every one of us thus to look upon ourselves as dying, and especially to think of it when we are sick. We are dying, that is, (1.) Our life is going; for the breath of life is going. It is continually <hi type="italic">going forth; it is in our nostrils</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.22">Isa. ii. 22</reference>), the door at which it entered (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen. ii. 7</reference>); there it is upon the threshold, ready to depart. Perhaps Job's distemper obstructed his breathing, and short breath will, after a while, be no breath. Let <hi type="italic">the Anointed of the Lord be the breath of our nostrils,</hi> and let us get spiritual life breathed into us, and that breath will never be corrupted. (2.) Our time is ending: <hi type="italic">My days are extinct, are put out,</hi> as a candle which, from the first lighting, is continually wasting and burning down, and will by degrees burn out of itself, but may by a thousand accidents be extinguished. Such is life. It concerns us therefore carefully to redeem the days of time, and to spend them in getting ready for the days of eternity, which will never be extinct. (3.) We are expected in our long home: <hi type="italic">The graves are ready for me.</hi> But would not one grave serve? Yes, but he speaks of the <hi type="italic">sepulchres of his fathers,</hi> to which he must be gathered: "The graves where they are laid are ready for me also," graves in consort, the congregation of the dead. Wherever we go there is but a step between us and the grave. Whatever is unready, that is ready; it is a bed soon made. If the graves be ready for us, it concerns us to be ready for the graves. <hi type="italic">The graves for me</hi> (so it runs), denoting not only his expectation of death, but his desire of it. "I have done with the world, and have nothing now to wish for but a grave." <div eID="gen9651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9652" type="x-p"/> 2. He was a despised man (<reference osisRef="Job.17.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He</hi>" (that is, Eliphaz, so some, or rather God, whom he all along acknowledges to be the author of his calamities) "<hi type="italic">has made me a byword of the people,</hi> the talk of the country, a laughing-stock to many, a gazing-stock to all; <hi type="italic">and aforetime</hi> (or to men's faces, publicly) <hi type="italic">I was as a tabret,</hi> that whoever chose might play upon." They made ballads of him; his name became a proverb; it is so still, <hi type="italic">As poor as Job.</hi> "<hi type="italic">He has</hi> now <hi type="italic">made me a byword,</hi>" a reproach of men, whereas, aforetime, in my prosperity, I was as a tabret, <hi type="italic">deliciæ humani generis—the darling of the human race,</hi> whom they were all pleased with. It is common for those who were honoured in their wealth to be despised in their poverty. <div eID="gen9652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9653" type="x-p"/> 3. He was a man of sorrows, <reference osisRef="Job.17.7">v. 7</reference>. He wept so much that he had almost lost his sight: <hi type="italic">My eye is dim by reason of sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.16.16">ch. xvi. 16</reference>. The sorrow of the world thus works darkness and death. He grieved so much that he had fretted all the flesh away and become a perfect skeleton, nothing but skin and bones: "<hi type="italic">All my members are as a shadow.</hi> I have become so poor and thin that I am not to be called a man, but the <hi type="italic">shadow of a man.</hi>" <div eID="gen9653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9654" type="x-p"/> II. The ill use which his friends made of his miseries. They trampled upon him, and insulted over him, and condemned him as a hypocrite, because he was thus grievously afflicted. Hard usage! Now observe, <div eID="gen9654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9655" type="x-p"/> 1. How Job describes it, and what construction he puts upon their discourses with him. He looks upon himself as basely abused by them. (1.) They abused him with their foul censures, condemning him as a bad man, justly reduced thus and exposed to contempt, <reference osisRef="Job.17.2">v. 2</reference>. "They are <hi type="italic">mockers,</hi> who deride my calamities, and insult over me, because I am thus brought low. They are <hi type="italic">so with me,</hi> abusing me to my face, pretending friendship in their visit, but intending mischief. I cannot get clear of them; they are continually tearing me, and they will not be wrought upon, either by reason or pity, to let fall the prosecution." (2.) They abused him too with their fair promises, for in them they did but banter him. He reckons them (<reference osisRef="Job.17.5">v. 5</reference>) among those that speak flattery to their friends. They all came to mourn with him. Eliphaz began with a commendation of him, <reference osisRef="Job.4.3">ch. iv. 3</reference>. They had all promised him that he would be happy if he would take their advice. Now all this he looked upon as flattery, and as designed to vex him so much the more. All this he calls their <hi type="italic">provocation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.17.2">v. 2</reference>. They did what they could to provoke him and then condemned him for his resentment of it; but he thinks himself excusable when his eye <hi type="italic">continued</hi> thus <hi type="italic">in their provocation:</hi> it never ceased, and he never could look off it. Note, The unkindness of those that trample upon their friends in affliction, that banter and abuse them then, is enough to try, if not to tire, the patience even of Job himself. <div eID="gen9655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9656" type="x-p"/> 2. How he condemns it. (1.) It was a sign that <hi type="italic">God had hidden their heart from understanding</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.17.4">v. 4</reference>), and that in this matter they were infatuated, and their wonted wisdom had departed from them. Wisdom is a gift of God, which he grants to some and withholds from others, grants at some times and withholds at other times. Those that are void of compassion are so far void of understanding. Where there is not the tenderness of a man one may question whether there be the understanding of a man. (2.) It would be a lasting reproach and diminution to them: <hi type="italic">Therefore shalt thou not exalt them.</hi> Those are certainly kept back from honour whose hearts are hidden from understanding. When God infatuates men he will abase them. Surely those who discover so little acquaintance with the methods of Providence shall not have the honour of deciding this controversy! That is reserved for a man of better sense and better temper, such a one as Elihu afterwards appeared to be. (3.) It would entail a curse upon their families. He that thus violates the sacred laws of friendship forfeits the benefit of it, not only for himself, but for his posterity: "<hi type="italic">Even the eyes of his children shall fail,</hi> and, when they look for succour and comfort from their own and their father's friends, they shall look in vain as I have done, and be as much disappointed as I am in you." Note, Those that wrong their neighbours may thereby, in the end, wrong their own children more than they are aware of. <div eID="gen9656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9657" type="x-p"/> 3. How he appeals from them to God (<reference osisRef="Job.17.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Lay down now, put me in a surety with thee,</hi> that is, "Let me be assured that God will take the hearing and determining of the cause into his own hands, and I desire no more. Let some one engage for God to bring on this matter." Thus those whose hearts condemn them not have confidence towards God, and can with humble and believing boldness beg of him to search and try them. Some make Job here to glance at the mediation of Christ, for he speaks of a surety with God, without whom he durst not appear before God, nor try his cause at his bar; for, though his friends' accusations of him were utterly false, yet he could not justify himself before God but in a mediator. Our English annotations give this reading of the verse: "<hi type="italic">Appoint, I pray thee, my surety with thee,</hi> namely, Christ who is with thee in heaven, and has undertaken to be my surety let him plead my cause, and stand up for me; and <hi type="italic">who is he then that will strike upon my hand?</hi>" that is, "Who dares then contend with me? Who shall lay any thing to my charge if Christ be an advocate for me?" <reference osisRef="Rom.8.32-Rom.8.33">Rom. viii. 32, 33</reference>. Christ is the surety of the better testament (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.22">Heb. vii. 22</reference>), a surety of God's appointing; and, if he undertake for us, we need not fear what can be done against us. <div eID="gen9657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9658" type="x-p"/> III. The good use which the righteous should make of Job's afflictions from God, from his enemies, and from his friends, <reference osisRef="Job.17.8-Job.17.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen9658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9659" type="x-p"/> 1. How the saints are described. (1.) They are <hi type="italic">upright men,</hi> honest and sincere, and that act from a steady principle, with a single eye. This was Job's own character (<reference osisRef="Job.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>), and probably he speaks of such upright men especially as had been his intimates and associates. (2.) They are <hi type="italic">the innocent,</hi> not perfectly so, but innocence is what they aim at and press towards. Sincerity is evangelical innocency, and those that are upright are said to be <hi type="italic">innocent from the great transgression,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.19.13">Ps. xix. 13</reference>. (3.) They are <hi type="italic">the righteous,</hi> who walk in the way of righteousness. (4.) They have <hi type="italic">clean hands,</hi> kept clean from the gross pollutions of sin, and, when spotted with infirmities, <hi type="italic">washed with innocency,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.26.6">Ps. xxvi. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen9659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9660" type="x-p"/> 2. How they should be affected with the account of Job's troubles. Great enquiry, no doubt, would be made concerning him, and every one would speak of him and his case; and what use will good people make of it? (1.) It will amaze them: <hi type="italic">Upright men shall be astonished at this;</hi> they will wonder to hear that so good a man as Job should be so grievously afflicted in body, name, and estate, that God should lay his hand so heavily upon him, and that his friends, who ought to have comforted him, should add to his grief, that such a remarkable saint should be such a remarkable sufferer, and so useful a man laid aside in the midst of his usefulness; what shall we say to these things? Upright men, though satisfied in general that God is wise and holy in all he does, yet cannot but be astonished at such dispensations of Providence, paradoxes which will not be unfolded till the mystery of God shall be finished. (2.) It will animate them. Instead of being deterred from and discouraged in the service of God, by the hard usage which this faithful servant of God met with, they shall be so much the more emboldened to proceed and persevere in it. That which was St. Paul's care (<reference osisRef="1Thess.3.3">1 Thess. iii. 3</reference>) was Job's, that no good man should be moved, either from his holiness or his comfort, by these afflictions, that none should, for the sake hereof, think the worse of the ways or work of God. And that which was St. Paul's comfort was his too, that <hi type="italic">the brethren in the Lord would wax confident by his bonds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.1.14">Phil. i. 14</reference>. They would hereby be animated, [1.] To oppose sin and to confront the corrupt and pernicious inferences which evil men would draw from Job's sufferings, as that God has forsaken the earth, that it is in vain to serve him, and the like: <hi type="italic">The innocent shall stir up himself against the hypocrite,</hi> will not bear to hear this (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.2">Rev. ii. 2</reference>), but will withstand him to his face, will stir up himself to search into the meaning of such providences and study these hard chapters, that he may read them readily, will stir up himself to maintain religion's just but injured cause against all its opposers. Note, The boldness of the attacks which profane people make upon religion should sharpen the courage and resolution of its friends and advocates. It is time to stir when proclamation is made in the gate of the camp, <hi type="italic">Who is on the Lord's side?</hi> When vice is daring it is no time for virtue, through fear, to hide itself. [2.] To persevere in religion. <hi type="italic">The righteous,</hi> instead of drawing back, or so much as starting back, at this frightful spectacle, or standing still to deliberate whether he should proceed or no (allude to <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.23">2 Sam. ii. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">shall</hi> with so much the more constancy and resolution <hi type="italic">hold on his way</hi> and press forward. "Though in me he foresees that bonds and afflictions abide him, <hi type="italic">yet none of these things shall move him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Acts xx. 24</reference>. Those who keep their eye upon heaven as their end will keep their feet in the paths of religion as their way, whatever difficulties and discouragements they meet with in it [3.] In order thereunto to grow in grace. He will not only hold on his way notwithstanding, but will grow <hi type="italic">stronger and stronger.</hi> By the sight of other good men's trials, and the experience of his own, he will be made more vigorous and lively in his duty, more warm and affectionate, more resolute and undaunted; the worse others are the better he will be; that which dismays others emboldens him. The blustering wind makes the traveller gather his cloak the closer about him and gird it the faster. Those that are truly wise and good will be continually growing wiser and better. Proficiency in religion is a good sign of sincerity in it.
entries.649131b8598dfc338761f88fa7b7ed619f503e7a: <div eID="gen9660" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job Reproves His Three Friends; Vanity of Worldly Expectations. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9661" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> But as for you all, do ye return, and come now: for I cannot find <hi type="italic">one</hi> wise <hi type="italic">man</hi> among you. <hi type="super">11</hi> My days are past, my purposes are broken off, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the thoughts of my heart. <hi type="super">12</hi> They change the night into day: the light <hi type="italic">is</hi> short because of darkness. <hi type="super">13</hi> If I wait, the grave <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine house: I have made my bed in the darkness. 14 I have said to corruption, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my father: to the worm, <hi type="italic">Thou art</hi> my mother, and my sister. <hi type="super">15</hi> And where <hi type="italic">is</hi> now my hope? as for my hope, who shall see it? 16 They shall go down to the bars of the pit, when <hi type="italic">our</hi> rest together <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the dust. <div eID="gen9661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9662" type="x-p"/> Job's friends had pretended to comfort him with the hopes of his return to a prosperous estate again; now he here shows, <div eID="gen9662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9663" type="x-p"/> I. That it was their folly to talk so (<reference osisRef="Job.17.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Return, and come now,</hi> be convinced that you are in an error, and let me persuade you to be of my mind; <hi type="italic">for I cannot find one wise man among you,</hi> that knows how to explain the difficulties of God's providence or how to apply the consolations of his promises." Those do not go wisely about the work of comforting the afflicted who fetch their comforts from the possibility of their recovery and enlargement in this world; though that is not to be despaired of, it is at the best uncertain; and if it should fail, as perhaps it may, the comfort built upon it will fail too. It is therefore our wisdom to comfort ourselves, and others, in distress, with that which will not fail, the promise of God, his love and grace, and a well-grounded hope of eternal life. <div eID="gen9663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9664" type="x-p"/> II. That it would he much more his folly to heed them; for, <div eID="gen9664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9665" type="x-p"/> 1. All his measures were already broken and he was full of confusion, <reference osisRef="Job.17.11-Job.17.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. He owns he had, in his prosperity, often pleased himself both with projects of what he should do and prospects of what he should enjoy; but now he looked upon his days as past, or drawing towards a period; all those purposes were broken off and those expectations dashed. He had had thoughts about enlarging his border, increasing his stock, and settling his children, and many pious thoughts, it is likely, of promoting religion in his country, redressing grievances, reforming the profane, relieving the poor, and raising funds perhaps for charitable uses; but he concluded that all these thoughts of his heart were now at an end, and that he should never have the satisfaction of seeing his designs effected. Note, The period of our days will be the period of all our contrivances and hopes for this world; but, if with full purpose of heart we cleave to the Lord, death will not break off that purpose. Job, being thus put upon new counsels, was under a constant uneasiness (<reference osisRef="Job.17.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The thoughts of his heart</hi> being broken, they <hi type="italic">changed the night into day and shortened the light.</hi> Some, in their vanity and riot, turn night into day and day into night; but Job did so through trouble and anguish of spirit, which were a hindrance, (1.) To the repose of the night, keeping his eyes waking, so that the night was as wearisome to him as the day, and the tossings of the night tired him as much as the toils of the day. (2.) To the entertainments of the day. "The light of the morning is welcome, but, by reason of this inward darkness, the comfort of it is soon gone, and the day is to me as dismal as the black and dark night," <reference osisRef="Deut.28.67">Deut. xxviii. 67</reference>. See what reason we have to be thankful for the health and ease which enable us to welcome both the shadows of the evening and the light of the morning. <div eID="gen9665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9666" type="x-p"/> 2. All his expectations from this world would very shortly be buried in the grave with him; so that it was a jest for him to think of such mighty things as they had flattered him with the hopes of, <reference osisRef="Job.5.19">ch. v. 19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.8.21">viii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">xi. 17</reference>. "Alas! you do but make a fool of me." <div eID="gen9666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9667" type="x-p"/> (1.) He saw himself just dropping into the grave. A convenient house, an easy bed, and agreeable relations, are some of those things in which we take satisfaction in this world: Job expected not any of these above ground; all he felt, and all he had in view, was unpleasing and disagreeable, but under ground he expected them. [1.] He counted upon no house but the grave (<reference osisRef="Job.17.13">v. 13</reference>): "If I wait, if there be any place where I shall ever be easy again, it must be in the grave. I should deceive myself if I should count upon any out-let from my trouble but what death will give me. Nothing is so sure as that." Note, In all our prosperity it is good to keep death in prospect. Whatever we expect, let us be sure to expect that; for that may prevent other things which we expect, but nothing will prevent that. But see how he endeavours not only to reconcile himself to the grave, but to recommend it to himself: "It is my house." The grave is a house; to the wicked it is a prison-house (<reference osisRef="Job.24.19-Job.24.20">ch. xxiv. 19, 20</reference>); to the godly it is <hi type="italic">Bethabara, a passage-house</hi> in their way home. "It is my house, mine by descent, I am born to it; it is my father's house. It is mine by purchase. I have made myself obnoxious to it." We must everyone of us shortly remove to this house, and it is our wisdom to provide accordingly; let us think of removing, and send before to our long home. [2.] He counted upon no quiet bed but in the darkness: "There," says he, "<hi type="italic">I have made my bed.</hi> It is made, for it is ready, and I am just going to it." The grave is a bed, for we shall rest in it in the evening of our day on earth, and rise from it in the morning of our everlasting day, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Isa. lvii. 2</reference>. Let this make good people willing to die; it is but going to bed; they are weary and sleepy, and it is time that they were in their beds. Why should they not go willingly, when their father calls? "Nay, <hi type="italic">I have made my bed,</hi> by preparation for it, have endeavoured to make it easy, by keeping conscience pure, by seeing Christ lying in this bed, and so turning it into a bed of spices, and by looking beyond it to the resurrection." [3.] He counted upon no agreeable relations but what he had in the grave (<reference osisRef="Job.17.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have cried to corruption</hi> (that is, to the grave, where the body will corrupt), <hi type="italic">Thou art my father</hi> (for our bodies were formed out of the earth), and <hi type="italic">to the worms</hi> there, <hi type="italic">You are my mother and my sister,</hi> to whom I am allied (for <hi type="italic">man is a worm</hi>) and with whom I must be conversant, for the <hi type="italic">worms shall cover us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.26">ch. xxi. 26</reference>. Job complained that his kindred were estranged from him (<reference osisRef="Job.19.13">ch. xix. 13, 14</reference>); therefore here he claims acquaintance with other relations that would cleave to him when those disowned him. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We are all of us near akin to corruption and the worms. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is therefore good to make ourselves familiar with them, by conversing much with them in our thoughts and meditations, which would very much help us above the inordinate love of life and fear of death. <div eID="gen9667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9668" type="x-p"/> (2.) He saw all his hopes from this world dropping into the grave with him (<reference osisRef="Job.17.15-Job.17.16">v. 15, 16</reference>): "Seeing I must shortly leave the world, <hi type="italic">where is now my hope?</hi> How can I expect to prosper who do not expect to live?" He is not hopeless, but his hope is not where they would have it be. <hi type="italic">If in this life only</hi> he had <hi type="italic">hope,</hi> he was <hi type="italic">of all men most miserable.</hi> "No, as for my hope, that hope which I comfort and support myself with, who shall see it? It is something out of sight that I hope for, not things that are seen, that are temporal, but things not seen, that are eternal." What is his hope he will tell us (<reference osisRef="Job.19.25">ch. xix. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">Non est mortale quod opto, immortale peto—I seek not for that which perishes, but for that which abides for ever.</hi> "But, as for the hopes you would buoy me up with, they shall go down with me to the bars of the pit. You are dying men, and cannot make good your promises. I am a dying man, and cannot enjoy the good you promise. Since, therefore, our rest will be together in the dust, let us all lay aside the thoughts of this world and set our hearts upon another." We must shortly be in the dust, for dust we are, dust and ashes in the pit, under <hi type="italic">the bars of the pit,</hi> held fast there, never to loose the bands of death till the general resurrection. But we shall rest there; we shall rest together there. Job and his friends could not agree now, but they will both be quiet in the grave; the dust of that will shortly stop their mouths and put an end to the controversy. Let the foresight of this cool the heat of all contenders and moderate the disputers of this world.  <chapter eID="Job.17"/> <div eID="gen9668" type="x-p"/>

entries.fd4b71c1e045f92ebeb479a22d168ca5b9b0d49a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4810"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 17</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.17.1-Job.17.16">Job 17:1-16</reference>. Job's Answer Continued.</title> <div sID="gen7020" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4810"/><hi type="bold">1. breath ... corrupt--</hi>result of elephantiasis. But Umbreit, "my strength (spirit) is spent."<div eID="gen7020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">extinct--</hi>Life is compared to an expiring light. "The light of my day is extinguished."<div eID="gen7021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7022" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">graves--</hi>plural, to heighten the force. <div eID="gen7022" type="x-p"/>
entries.c57f54d8b4695757bec38ffaf20f6d18e880e11c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4811"/><div sID="gen7023" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4811"/>2. Umbreit, more emphatically, "had I only not to endure mockery, in the midst of their contentions I (mine eye) would remain quiet."<div eID="gen7023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eye continue--</hi>Hebrew, "tarry all night"; a figure taken from sleep at night, to express undisturbed rest; opposed to (<reference osisRef="Job.16.20">Job 16:20</reference>), when the eye of Job is represented as pouring out tears to God without rest. <div eID="gen7024" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7deeb0d182c166ab307cd506c1ecba865540835: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4812"/><div sID="gen7025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4812"/><hi type="bold">3. Lay down now--</hi>namely, a pledge or security; that is, be my surety; do Thou attest my innocence, since my friends only mock me (<reference osisRef="Job.17.2">Job 17:2</reference>). Both litigating parties had to lay down a sum as security before the trial.<div eID="gen7025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7026" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">put me in a surety--</hi>Provide a surety for me (in the trial) with Thee. A presage of the "surety" (<reference osisRef="Heb.7.22">He 7:22</reference>), or "one Mediator between God and man" (see on <reference osisRef="Job.16.21">Job 16:21</reference>).<div eID="gen7026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strike hands--</hi>"who else (save God Himself) could strike hands with me?" that is, be my security (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.122">Psa 119:122</reference>). The Hebrew strikes the hand of him for whom he goes security (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.1">Pr 6:1</reference>). <div eID="gen7027" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc17f40597f7e8500ba6c27a79213eba4963abcb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4813"/><div sID="gen7028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4813"/><hi type="bold">4. their heart--</hi>The intellect of his friends.<div eID="gen7028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shalt ... exalt--</hi>Rather imperative, "exalt them not"; allow them not to conquer [Umbreit], (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Is 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen7029" type="x-p"/>
entries.e97484b04ce64370c8f8f3e842cae1a102fa4826: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4814"/><div sID="gen7030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4814"/>5. The Hebrew for "flattery" is "smoothness"; then it came to mean a prey divided by lot, because a smooth stone was used in casting the lots (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.8">De 18:8</reference>), "a portion" (<reference osisRef="Gen.14.24">Ge 14:24</reference>). Therefore translate, "He that delivers up his friend as a prey (which the conduct of my friends implies that they would do), even the eyes," &c. [Noyes] (<reference osisRef="Job.11.20">Job 11:20</reference>). Job says this as to the sinner's children, retorting upon their reproach as to the cutting off of his (<reference osisRef="Job.5.4">Job 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.30">15:30</reference>). This accords with the Old Testament dispensation of legal retribution (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7030" type="x-p"/>
entries.db6d2760bb822fb6ad76f19ff00d61db41dde43e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4815"/><div sID="gen7031" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4815"/><hi type="bold">6. He--</hi>God. The poet reverentially suppresses the name of God when speaking of calamities inflicted.<div eID="gen7031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7032" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by-word--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.28.37">De 28:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.11">Psa 69:11</reference>). My awful punishment makes my name execrated everywhere, as if I must have been superlatively bad to have earned it.<div eID="gen7032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">aforetime ... tabret--</hi>as David was honored (<reference osisRef="1Sam.18.6">1Sa 18:6</reference>). Rather from a different Hebrew root, "I am treated to my face as an object of disgust," literally, "an object to be spit upon in the face" (<reference osisRef="Num.12.14">Nu 12:14</reference>). So Raca means (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.22">Mt 5:22</reference>) [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7033" type="x-p"/>
entries.981d13037ed5d9466362bca2f93e9ae2dae93927: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4816"/><div sID="gen7034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4816"/>7. (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.9">31:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.34.7">De 34:7</reference>).<div eID="gen7034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">members--</hi>literally, "figures"; all the individual members being peculiar forms of the body; opposed to "shadow," which looks like a figure without solidity. <div eID="gen7035" type="x-p"/>
entries.46768fb79e9712f0aee6e7a40bab3a48efd301bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4817"/><div sID="gen7036" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4817"/><hi type="bold">8. astonied--</hi>at my unmerited sufferings.<div eID="gen7036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7037" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">against the hypocrite--</hi>The upright shall feel their sense of justice wounded ("will be indignant") because of the prosperity of the wicked. By "hypocrite" or "ungodly," he perhaps glances at his false friends. <div eID="gen7037" type="x-p"/>
entries.80f2a9fb67c0a1826544a1dede014d4d59ff2511: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4818"/><div sID="gen7038" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4818"/>9. The strength of religious principle is heightened by misfortune. The pious shall take fresh courage to persevere from the example of suffering Job. The image is from a warrior acquiring new courage in action (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.30">Is 40:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.14">Php 1:14</reference>). <div eID="gen7038" type="x-p"/>
entries.728e271ce7fb51f6a1e6c56c6f27aa34e78c59e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4819"/><div sID="gen7039" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4819"/><hi type="bold">10. return--</hi>If you have anything to advance really wise, though I doubt it, recommence your speech. For as yet I cannot find one wise man among you all. <div eID="gen7039" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ddf7071ee12ca8708d4939db280adb4698341bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4820"/><div sID="gen7040" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4820"/>11. Only do not vainly speak of the restoration of health to me; for "my days are past."<div eID="gen7040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7041" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">broken off--</hi>as the threads of the web cut off from the loom (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.12">Is 38:12</reference>).<div eID="gen7041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thoughts--</hi>literally, "possessions," that is, all the feelings and fair hopes which my heart once nourished. These belong to the heart, as "purposes" to the understanding; the two together here describe the entire inner man. <div eID="gen7042" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca0ca9e0e5939fc1cf21adf3b512d80b41fba9dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4821"/><div sID="gen7043" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4821"/><hi type="bold">12. They--</hi>namely, "my friends."<div eID="gen7043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">change the night into day--</hi>that is, would try to persuade me of the change of my misery into joy, which is impossible [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>); (but) the light of prosperity (could it be enjoyed) would be short because of the darkness of adversity. Or better for "short," the Hebrew "near"; "and the light of new prosperity should be near in the face of (before) the darkness of death"; that is, they would persuade me that light is near, even though darkness approaches. <div eID="gen7044" type="x-p"/>
entries.be23d1199e3e11eef373afee18b5168db3b3ec4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4822"/><div sID="gen7045" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4822"/>13. Rather, "if I wait for this grave (Sheol, or the unseen world) as my house, and make my bed in the darkness (<reference osisRef="Job.17.14">Job 17:14</reference>), and say to corruption," rather, "to the pit" or "grave," &c. (<reference osisRef="Job.17.15">Job 17:15</reference>). Where then is my hope? [Umbreit]. The apodosis is at <reference osisRef="Job.17.15">Job 17:15</reference>. <div eID="gen7045" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ac625551f15015cff1352913abe33e1f7198bc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4823"/><div sID="gen7046" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4823"/><hi type="bold">14. Thou art my father, &c.--</hi>expressing most intimate connection (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.4">Pr 7:4</reference>). His diseased state made him closely akin to the grave and worm. <div eID="gen7046" type="x-p"/>
entries.d7f37dc081c6ff9eeac47f702f6a939f0ded1c95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4824"/><div sID="gen7047" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4824"/>15. Who shall see it fulfilled? namely, the "hope" (<reference osisRef="Job.11.18">Job 11:18</reference>) which they held out to him of restoration. <div eID="gen7047" type="x-p"/>
entries.a6c0ca4962e2ec0e39f1f20ce4dd3ab38f6e6f66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4825"/><div sID="gen7048" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4825"/><hi type="bold">16. They--</hi>namely, my hopes shall be buried with me.<div eID="gen7048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7049" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bars--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.38.10">Is 38:10</reference>). Rather, the wastes or solitudes of the pit (sheol, the unseen world).<div eID="gen7049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7050" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rest together--</hi>the rest of me and my hope is in, &c. Both expire together. The word "rest" implies that man's ceaseless hopes only rob him of rest. <chapter eID="Job.17"/>

entries.c665bff13571b18ae739c7e4d37b9c16755226d6: <div eID="gen16666" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen16667" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16668" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16668" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16667" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16669" type="x-p"/> Job complains of the injustice of his friends, and compares his present state of want and wo with his former honor and affluence, <reference osisRef="Job.17.1-Job.17.6">Job 17:1-6</reference>. God's dealings with him will ever astonish upright men; yet the righteous shall not be discouraged, but hold on his way, <reference osisRef="Job.17.7-Job.17.9">Job 17:7-9</reference>. Asserts that there is not a wise man among his friends, and that he has no expectation but of a speedy death, <reference osisRef="Job.17.10-Job.17.16">Job 17:10-16</reference>. <div eID="gen16669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16670" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen16670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16671" type="x-p"/> My breath is corrupt - Rather, My spirit is oppressed, רוחי חבלה ruchi chubbalah: My days are extinct, and the sepulchral cells are ready for me - Parkhurst. There is probably a reference here to cemeteries, where were several niches, in Each of which a corpse was deposited. See on <reference osisRef="Job.17.16">Job 17:16</reference> (note). For חבלה chubbalah, corrupted or oppressed, some MSS. have חלה chalah, is made weak; and one has גבלה is worn down, consumed: this is agreeable to the Vulgate, Spiritus meus attenuebatur; "My spirit is exhausted."
entries.d1ccfb75b87f8b149be75eeca13ecf0f43c558bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen16671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16672" type="x-p"/> Are there not mockers with me? - This has been variously translated. The Vulgate: "I have not sinned, and yet my eye dwells upon afflictions." Septuagint: "I conjure you, laboring under afflictions, what evil have I done? Yet strangers have robbed me of my substance." Mr. Good: "But are not revilers before me? Alas, mine eye penetrateth their rebukes." Calmet thinks the Hebrew might be translated thus: "If I have not been united in friendship with the wicked, why are my eyes in bitterness?" Coverdale translates both verses thus: My breth fayleth, my dayes are shortened, I am harde at deathes dore. I have disceaved no man, yet must myne eye continue in hevynesse. Mr. Heath "Were it not so, I have sarcasms enow in store; and I could spend the whole night unmoved at their aggravations." The general meaning is sufficiently plain, and the reader has got translations enough.
entries.ae763204cc876db3858dbb6026000e0471e6990b: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen16672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16673" type="x-p"/> Lay down now - Deposit a pledge; stake your conduct against mine, and your life and soul on the issue; let the cause come before God, let him try it; and see whether any of you shall be justified by him, while I am condemned.
entries.010dfdf2dfb9da11fdce9e041c7215bdcc3b2756: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen16673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16674" type="x-p"/> For thou hast hid their heart - This address is to God; and here he is represented as doing that which in the course of his providence he only permits to be done. <div eID="gen16674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16675" type="x-p"/> Shalt thou not exalt them - This was exactly fulfilled: not one of Job's friends was exalted; on the contrary, God condemned the whole; and they were not received into the Divine favor till Job sacrificed, and made intercession for them.
entries.96c7b0c8251e2f8749f06ea6b5ee24305a0d2746: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen16675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16676" type="x-p"/> He that speaketh flattery - There is a great variety of meaning given to the terms in this verse. The general sense is, The man who expects much from his friends will be disappointed: while depending on them his children's eyes may fail in looking for bread.
entries.870cff2fd08e8e78e5115476ffae6499ae6600b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen16676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16677" type="x-p"/> He hath made me also a by-word - My afflictions and calamities have become a subject of general conversation, so that my poverty and affliction are proverbial. As poor as Job, As afflicted as Job, are proverbs that have even reached our times and are still in use. <div eID="gen16677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16678" type="x-p"/> Aforetime I was as a tabret - This is not the translation of the Hebrew ותפת לפנים אהיה vethopheth lephanim eheyeh. Instead of לפנים lephanim, I would read לפניהם liphneghem, and then the clause might be translated thus: I shall be as a furnace, or consuming fire (Topheth) before them. They shall have little reason to mock when they see the end of the Lord's dealings with me; my example will be a consuming fire to them, and my false friends will be confounded. Coverdale translates thus: He hath made me as it were a byworde of the comon people. I am his gestinge stocke amonge them.
entries.063e03024b9b72829e6de4732fe75b6723534fcc: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen16678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16679" type="x-p"/> Mine eye also is dim - Continual weeping impairs the sight; and indeed any affliction that debilitates the frame generally weakens the sight in the same proportion. <div eID="gen16679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16680" type="x-p"/> All my members are as a shadow - Nothing is left but skin and bone. I am but the shadow of my former self.
entries.240beaeb99c60d8d65598e4e446a669ef771075e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen16680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16681" type="x-p"/> Upright men shall be astonied - In several of these verses Job is supposed to speak prophetically of his future restoration, and of the good which religious society should derive from the history of his original affluence, consequent poverty and affliction, and final restoration to health, peace, and prosperity. The upright will receive the account with astonishment, and wonder at the dispensations of the Almighty; while hypocrites, false professors and the sour-headed, godly, shall be unmasked, and innocent men, whether in affliction or affluence, shall be known to be favourites of the Almighty.
entries.03945aaddaf38a1bd84cf5c168928440ddbaddf6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen16681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16682" type="x-p"/> The righteous also shall hold on his way - There shall be no doubt concerning the dispensations of the Divine providence. My case shall illustrate all seemingly intricate displays of God's government. None shall be stumbled at seeing a godly man under oppression, knowing that God never permits any thing of the kind but for the good of the subject, and the manifestation of his own mercy, wisdom, and love. Therefore whatever occurs to the righteous man, he will take it for granted that all is well and justly managed, and that the end will be glorious. <div eID="gen16682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16683" type="x-p"/> Shall be stronger and stronger - He shall take encouragement from my case, stay himself on the Lord, and thus gain strength by every blast of adversity. This is one grand use of the book of Job. It casts much light on seemingly partial displays of Divine providence: and has ever been the great text-book of godly men in a state of persecution and affliction. This is what Job seems prophetically to declare.
entries.aae76bfd3825492c57cf969104fecf7ffde3b2e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen16683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16684" type="x-p"/> But as for you all - Ye are too proud, and too full of self-importance, to profit by what ye see. Return - enter into yourselves, consider your ways, go again to school, get back to your own houses, and endeavor to acquire humility and knowledge; for there is not one wise man among you.
entries.1646efcd14f89bed8e41230015f15c606daae3c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen16684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16685" type="x-p"/> My days are past - Job seems to relapse here into his former state of gloom. These transitions are very frequent in this poem; and they strongly mark the struggle of piety and resignation with continued affliction, violent temptation, and gloomy providences. <div eID="gen16685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16686" type="x-p"/> The thoughts of my heart - All my purposes are interrupted; and all my schemes and plans, in relation to myself and family, are torn asunder, destroyed, and dissipated.
entries.c052175a19a504296c2bb3930867bcd7cc5a3bce: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen16686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16687" type="x-p"/> They change the night into day - These purposes and thoughts are so very gloomy, that they change day into night. <div eID="gen16687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16688" type="x-p"/> The light is short because of darkness - אור קרוב מפני חשך or karob mippeney choshek, "The light is near from the face of darkness." I have scarcely any light: what is called light is so near akin to darkness, that it is scarcely severed from it. There is either no light, or merely such as is sufficient to render darkness visible. A fine picture of the state of his mind - he was generally in darkness; but had occasional gleams of hope.
entries.d4db27eda73902d9dfc068efd98e5bb65b80b9fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen16688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16689" type="x-p"/> The grave is mine house - Let my life be long or short, the grave at last will be my home. I expect soon to lie down in darkness - there is my end: I cannot reasonably hope for any thing else.
entries.87e7df9ddf69d7633c9baba31c4797e9369935f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen16689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16690" type="x-p"/> I have said to corruption - I came from a corrupted stock, and I must go to corruption again. The Hebrew might be thus rendered: To the ditch I have called, Thou art my father. To the worm, Thou art my mother and my sister. I am in the nearest state of affinity to dissolution and corruption: I may well call them my nearest relations, as I shall soon be blended with them.
entries.2d9325575fc886dcd9e1a436034a1f02386d56ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen16690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16691" type="x-p"/> And where is now my hope? - In the circumstances in which I am found, of what use can hope be? Were I to form the expectation of future good, who could ever see it realized? Is it then any wonder that I should complain and bemoan my wretched lot?
entries.05b9bc92ae66c8886f0fb6219e7d3130993b9023: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen16691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16692" type="x-p"/> They shall go down to the bars of the pit - All that I have must descend into the depths of the grave. Thither are we all going; and there alone can I rest. בדי baddey, which we translate bars, signifies also branches, distended limbs, or claws, and may here refer either to a personification of the grave, a monster who seizes on human bodies, and keeps them fast in his deadly gripe; or to the different branching-off-alleys in subterranean cemeteries, or catacombs, in which niches are made for the reception of different bodies. <div eID="gen16692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16693" type="x-p"/> When our rest together is in the dust - That is, according to some critics, My hope and myself shall descend together into the grave. It shall never be realized, for the time of my departure is at hand. <div eID="gen16693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16694" type="x-p"/> In those times what deep shades hung on the state of man after death, and on every thing pertaining to the eternal world! Perplexity and uncertainty were the consequences; and a corresponding gloom often dwelt on the minds of even the best of the Old Testament believers. Job's friends, though learned in all the wisdom of the Arabians, connected with the advantages derivable from the Mosaic writings, and perhaps those of the earlier prophets, had little clear or distinct in their minds relative to all subjects post mortem, or of the invisible world. Job himself, though sometimes strongly confident, is often harassed with doubts and fears upon the subject, insomuch that his sayings and experience often appear contradictory. Perhaps it could not be otherwise; the true light was not then come: Jesus alone brought life and immortality to light by his Gospel.  <chapter eID="Job.17"/> <div eID="gen16694" type="x-p"/>

entries.097116d316941e85e88ef0076243360f6b3307a0: <reference osisRef="Job.17.1-Job.2.1">Job 17:1-2   1</reference>  My breath is corrupt, <div eID="gen7559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7560" type="x-p"/> My days are extinct, <div eID="gen7560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7561" type="x-p"/> The graves are ready for me.   2  Truly mockery surrounds me, <div eID="gen7561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7562" type="x-p"/> And mine eye shall loiter over their disputings. <div eID="gen7562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7563" type="x-p"/> Hirz., Hlgst., and others, wrongly consider the division of the chapter here to be incorrect. The thought in <reference osisRef="Job.16.22">Job 16:22</reference> is really a concluding thought, like Job 10:20., Job 7:21. Then in <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job 17:1</reference> another strain is taken up; and as <reference osisRef="Job.16.22">Job 16:22</reference> is related, as a confirmation, to the request expressed in <reference osisRef="Job.16.19-Job.16.21">Job 16:19-21</reference>, so <reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job 17:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.17.2">Job 17:2</reference> are related to that expressed in Job 17:3. The connection with the conclusion of Job 16 is none the less close: the thoughts move on somewhat crosswise (<hi type="italic">chiastisch</hi>). We do not translate with Ewald: “My spirit is destroyed,” because חבּל (here and <reference osisRef="Isa.10.27">Isa 10:27</reference>) signifies not, to be destroyed, but, to be corrupted, disturbed, troubled; not the spirit (after Arab. <hi type="italic">chbl</hi>, usually of disturbance of spirit), but the breath is generally meant, which is become short (<reference osisRef="Job.7.15">Job 7:15</reference>) and offensive (<reference osisRef="Job.19.17">Job 19:17</reference>), announcing suffocation and decay as no longer far distant. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job 17:1</reference></hi> the ἅπ. γεγρ. נזעכוׁ is equivalent to נדעכו, found elsewhere. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job 17:1</reference></hi> קברים is used as if the dead were called, Arab. <hi type="italic">ssâchib el - kubûr</hi>, grave-companions. He is indeed one who is dying, from whom the grave is but a step distant, and still the friends promise him long life if he will only repent! This is the mockery which is with him, i.e., surrounds him, as he affirms, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.17.1">Job 17:1</reference></hi>. A secondary verb, התל, is formed from the <hi type="italic">Hiph.</hi> התל (of which we had the non-syncopated form of the <hi type="italic">fut.</hi> in <reference osisRef="Job.13.9">Job 13:9</reference>), the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> of which occurs in 1Ki 18:27 of Elijah’s derision of the priests of Baal, and from this is formed the <hi type="italic">pluralet</hi>. התלים (or, according to another reading, התלּים, with the same doubling of the ל as in מהתלּות, deceitful things, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.10">Isa 30:10</reference>; comp. the same thing in <reference osisRef="Job.33.7">Job 33:7</reference>, אראלּם, their lions of God = heroes), which has the meaning foolery, - a meaning questioned by Hirz. without right, - in which the idea of deceit and mockery are united. Gecatilia and Ralbag take it as a <hi type="italic">part.:</hi> mockers; Stick., Wolfson, Hahn: deluded; but the analogy of שׁעשׁעים, תעלולים, and the like, speaks in favour of taking it as a substantive. אם־לא is affirmative (Ges. §155, 2, <hi type="italic">f</hi>). Ewald renders it as expressive of desire: if only not (Hlgst.: <hi type="italic">dummodo ne</hi>); but this signification (Ew. §329, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) cannot be supported. On the other hand, it might be intended interrogatively (as <reference osisRef="Job.30.25">Job 30:25</reference>): <hi type="italic">annon illusiones mecum</hi> (Rosenm.); but this אם־לא, corresponding to the second member of a disjunctive question, has no right connection in the preceding. We therefore prefer the affirmative meaning, and explain it like <reference osisRef="Job.22.20">Job 22:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.36">Job 31:36</reference>, comp. Job 2:5. Truly what he continually hears, i.e., from the side of the friends, is only false and delusive utterances, which consequently sound to him like jesting and mockery. The suff. in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.17.2">Job 17:2</reference></hi> refers to them. המּרות (with <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens</hi>, which renders the sound of the word more pathetic, as <reference osisRef="Job.9.18">Job 9:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.1.17">Joe 1:17</reference>, and in the <hi type="italic">Hiph.</hi> form כנּלתך, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa 33:1</reference>), elsewhere generally (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.18">Jos 1:18</reference> only excepted) of rebellion against God, denotes here the contradictory, quarrelsome bearing of the friends, not the dispute in itself (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">mry ,</hi> III. to attack, VI. to contend with another), but coming forward controversially; only to this is תּלן עיני suitable. הלין must not be taken as = הלּין here; Ewald’s translation, “only let not mine eye come against their irritation,” forces upon this verb, which always signifies to murmur, γογγύζειν, a meaning foreign to it, and one that does not well suit it here. The voluntative form תּלן = תּלן (here not the pausal form, as Jdg 19:20, comp. <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.16">2Sa 17:16</reference>) quite accords with the sense: mine eye shall linger on their janglings; it shall not look on anything that is cheering, but be held fast by this cheerless spectacle, which increases his bodily suffering and his inward pain. From these comforters, who are become his adversaries, Job turns in supplication to God.
entries.c13f309e2dc8a689b826c7e20b6922b3eb1ba6b7: <reference osisRef="Job.17.3-Job.5.3">Job 17:3-5   3</reference>  Lay down now, be bondsman for me with Thyself; <div eID="gen7563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7564" type="x-p"/> Who else should furnish surety to me?!   4  For Thou hast closed their heart from understanding, <div eID="gen7564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7565" type="x-p"/> Therefore wilt Thou not give authority to them.   5  He who giveth his friends for spoil, <div eID="gen7565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7566" type="x-p"/> The eyes of his children shall languish. <div eID="gen7566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7567" type="x-p"/> It is unnecessary, with Reiske and Olsh., to read ערבני (<hi type="italic">pone quaeso arrhabonem meum</hi> = <hi type="italic">pro me</hi>) in order that שׂימה may not stand without an object; שׂימה has this meaning included in it, and the ארבני which follows shows that neither לבך (Ralbag) nor ידך (Carey) is to be supplied; accordingly שׂים here, like Arab. <hi type="italic">wḍ‛</hi> (<hi type="italic">wâḍ‛</hi>), and in the classics both τιθέναι and <hi type="italic">ponere</hi>, signifies alone the laying down of a pledge. Treated by the friends as a criminal justly undergoing punishment, he seeks his refuge in God, who has set the mark of a horrible disease upon him contrary to his desert, as though he were guilty, and implores Him to confirm the reality of his innocence in some way or other by laying down a pledge for him (ὑποθήκη). The further prayer is ערבני, as word of entreaty which occurs also in Hezekiah’s psalm, <reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Isa 38:14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.119.122">Psa 119:122</reference>; ערב <hi type="italic">seq. acc. </hi>signifies, as noted on the latter passage, to furnish surety for any one, and gen. to take the place of a mediator (comp. also on <reference osisRef="Heb.7.22">Heb 7:22</reference>, where ἔγγυος is a synon. of μεσίτης). Here, however, the significant עמּך is added: furnish security for me with Thyself; elsewhere the form is ל ערב, to furnish security for (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.1">Pro 6:1</reference>), or לפני before, any one, here with עם of the person by whom the security is to be accepted. The thought already expressed in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.16.21">Job 16:21</reference></hi> receives a still stronger expression here: God is conceived of as two persons, on the one side as a judge who treats Job as one deserving of punishment, on the other side as a bondsman who pledges himself for the innocence of the sufferer before the judge, and stands as it were as surety against the future. In the question, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.17.3">Job 17:3</reference></hi>, the representation is again somewhat changed: Job appears here as the one to whom surety is given. נתקע, described by expositors as reciprocal, is rather reflexive: to give one’s hand (the only instance of the <hi type="italic">med</hi>. form of כּף תּקע) = to give surety by striking hands, <hi type="italic">dextera data sponsionem in se recipere</hi> (Hlgst.). And לידי is not to be explained after the analogy of the passive, as the usual ל of the agents: who would allow himself to be struck by my hand, i.e., who would accept the surety from me (Wolfson), which is unnatural both in representation and expression; but it is, according to <reference osisRef="Prov.6.1">Pro 6:1</reference> (vid., Bertheau), intended of the hand of him who receives the stroke of the hand of him who gives the pledge. This is therefore the meaning of the question: who else (הוּא מי), if not God himself, should strike (his hand) to my hand, i.e., should furnish to me a pledge (viz., of my innocence) by joining hands? There is none but God alone who can intercede for him, as a guarantee of his innocence before himself and others. This negative answer: None but Thou alone, is established in Job 17:4. God has closed the heart of the friends against understanding, prop. concealed, i.e., He has fixed a curtain, a wall of partition, between their hearts and the right understanding of the matter; He has smitten them with blindness, therefore He will not (since they are suffering from a want of perception which He has ordained, and which is consequently known to Him) allow them to be exalted, i.e., to conquer and triumph. “The exaltation of the friends,” observes Hirzel rightly, “would be, that God should openly justify their assertion of Job’s guilt.” Löwenthal translates: therefore art thou not honoured; but it is not pointed תּרמם = תּתרמם, but תּרמם, whether it be that אתם is to be supplied, or that it is equivalent to תּרממם (Ew. §62, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, who, however, prefers to take is as <hi type="italic">n. Hithpa.</hi> like תּקמם in the unimproved signification: improvement, since he maintains this affords no right idea), according to the analogy of similar verb-forms (<reference osisRef="Job.31.15">Job 31:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.6">Isa 64:6</reference>), by a resolving of the two similar consonants which occur together. <div eID="gen7567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7568" type="x-p"/> The hope thus expressed Job establishes (<reference osisRef="Job.17.5">Job 17:5</reference>) by a principle from general experience, that he who offers his friends as spoil for distribution will be punished most severely for the same upon his children: he shall not escape the divine retribution which visits him, upon his own children, for the wrong done to his friends. Almost all modern expositors are agreed in this rendering of לחלק as regards <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.17.5">Job 17:5</reference></hi>; but חלק must not be translated “lot” (Ewald), which it never means; it signifies a share of spoil, as e.g., Num 31:36 (Jerome <hi type="italic">praedam</hi>), or even with a verbal force: plundering (from חלק,   <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.21">2Ch 28:21</reference>), or even in antithesis to entering into bond for a friend with all that one possesses (Stick., Schlottm.), a dividing (of one’s property) = distraining, as a result of the surrender to the creditor, to which the verb הגּיד is appropriate, which would then denote denouncing before a court of justice, as <reference osisRef="Jer.20.10">Jer 20:10</reference>, not merely proclaiming openly, as Isa 3:9. We have translated “spoil,” which admits of all these modifications and excludes none; the general meaning is certainly: one deserts (instead of shielding as an intercessor) his friends and delivers them up; יגּיד with a general subj., as <reference osisRef="Job.4.2">Job 4:2</reference> (if any one attempts), <reference osisRef="Job.15.3">Job 15:3</reference>; Job 27:23. With respect to the other half of the verse, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.17.5">Job 17:5</reference></hi>, the optative rendering: may they languish (Vaih.), to the adoption of which the old expositors have been misled by parallels like Psa 109:9., is to be rejected; it is contrary to the character of Job (<reference osisRef="Job.31.30">Job 31:30</reference>). We agree with Mercerus: <hi type="italic">Nequaquam hoc per imprecationem, sed ut consequentis justissimae poenae denunciationem ab Iobo dictum putamus.</hi> For v. 5 <hi type="italic">b</hi> is also not to be taken as a circumstantial clause: even if the eyes of his children languish (Ew., Hlgst. Stick., Hahn, Schl.). It is not רעהוּ, but רעים; and before supposing here a <hi type="italic">Synallage num</hi>. so liable to be misunderstood, one must try to get over the difficulty without it, which is here easy enough. Hence Job is made, in the intended application of the general principle, to allude to his own children, and Ewald really considers him the father of infant children, which, however, as may be seen from the prologue, is nothing but an invention unsupported by the history. Since it is בניו and not בניהם, we refer the suff. to the subj. of יגיד. The <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of ועיני Mich. calls <hi type="italic">Waw consecutivum;</hi> it, however, rather combines things that are inseparable (certainly as cause and effect, sin and punishment). And it is יגיד, not הגיד, because the <hi type="italic">perf.</hi> would describe the fact as past, while the <hi type="italic">fut.</hi> places us in the midst of this faithless conduct. Job says God cannot possibly allow these, his three friends, the upper hand. One proclaims his friends as spoil (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.6.27">Job 6:27</reference>), and the eyes of his children languish (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.11.20">Job 11:20</reference>), i.e., he who so faithlessly disowns the claims of affection, is punished for it on that which he holds most dear. But this uncharitableness which he experiences is also a visitation of God. In the next strophe he refers all that he meets with from man to Him as the final cause, but not without a presage of the purpose for which it is designed.
entries.94051730800399d687f10549e10a95de4853085a: <reference osisRef="Job.17.6-Job.9.6">Job 17:6-9   6</reference>  And He hath made me a proverb to the world, <div eID="gen7568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7569" type="x-p"/> And I became as one in whose face they spit.   7  Then mine eye became dim with grief, <div eID="gen7569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7570" type="x-p"/> And all my members were like a shadow.   8  The upright were astonished at it, <div eID="gen7570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7571" type="x-p"/> And the innocent is stirred up over the godless;   9  Nevertheless the righteous holdeth fast on his way, <div eID="gen7571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7572" type="x-p"/> And he that hath clean hands waxeth stronger and stronger. <div eID="gen7572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7573" type="x-p"/> Without a question, the subj. of <reference osisRef="Job.17.6">Job 17:6</reference> is God. It is the same thing whether משׁל is taken as <hi type="italic">inf.</hi> followed by the subject in the nominative (Ges. §133, 2), or as a subst. (lxx θρύλλημα; Aq., Symm., Theod., παραβολήν), like שׂחוק, <reference osisRef="Job.12.4">Job 12:4</reference>, followed by the <hi type="italic">gen. subjectivus</hi>. משׁל is the usual word for ridicule, expressed in parables of a satirical character, e.g., <reference osisRef="Joel.2.17">Joe 2:17</reference> (according to which, if משׁל were intended as <hi type="italic">inf.,</hi> משׁל־בּי עמּים might have been expected); עמּים signifies both nations and races, and tribes or people, i.e., members of this and that nation, or in gen. of mankind (<reference osisRef="Job.12.2">Job 12:2</reference>). We have intentionally chosen an ambiguous expression in the translation, for what Job says can be meant of a wide range of people (comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.2.11">Job 2:11</reference> <hi type="italic">ad fin.</hi>), as well as of those in the immediate neighbourhood; the friends themselves represent different tribes; and a perishable gipsy-like troglodyte race, to whom Job is become a derision, is specially described further on (Job 24, 30).  <reference osisRef="Job.17.6">Job 17:6</reference> <div eID="gen7573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7574" type="x-p"/> By תּפת (translated by Jer. <hi type="italic">exemplum</hi>, and consequently mistaken for מופת) the older expositors are reminded of the name of the place where the sacrifices were offered to Moloch in the valley of the sons of Hinnom (whence גּיהנּם, γέεννα, hell), since they explain it by “the fire of hell,” but only from want of a right perception; the לפנים standing with it, which nowhere signifies <hi type="italic">palam</hi>, and cannot here (where אהיה, although in the signification ἐγενόμην, follows) signify <hi type="italic">a multo tempore,</hi> shows that תפת here is to be derived from תּוּף, to spit out (as נפת, gum, from נוּף). This verb certainly cannot be supported in Hebr. and Aram. (since רקק is the commoner word), except two passages in the Talmud (<hi type="italic">Nidda</hi> 42 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, comp. <hi type="italic">Sabbath</hi> 99 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Chethuboth</hi> 61 <hi type="italic">b</hi>); but it is confirmed by the Aethiopic and Coptic and an onomatopoetic origin, as the words πτύειν, ψύειν, <hi type="italic">spuere</hi>, Germ. <hi type="italic">speien</hi>, etc., show.<note placement="foot">תוף is related to the Sanskrit root <hi type="italic">shttı̂v</hi>, as τέγη, τρύχους, τρύζω, and the like, to στέγη, στρύχνος, στρύζω,, vid., Kuhn’s <hi type="italic">Zeitschrift</hi>, Bd. iv. Abh. i. (the falling away of <hi type="italic">s</hi> before mutes).</note> <div eID="gen7574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7575" type="x-p"/> Cognate is the Arabic <hi type="italic">taffafa</hi>, to treat with contempt, and the interjection <hi type="italic">tuffan</hi>, fie upon thee,<note placement="foot">Almost all modern expositors repeat the remark here, that this <hi type="italic">tuffan</hi> is similar in meaning to ῥακά, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.22">Mat 5:22</reference>, while they might learn from Lightfoot that it has nothing to do with רק, to spit, but is equivalent to ריקא, κενέ.</note> e.g., in the proverb (quoted by Umbreit): <hi type="italic">‛aini fihi watuffan ‛aleihi</hi>, my eye rests on it wishfully, and yet I feel disgust at it. Therefore לפנים (spitting upon the face) is equivalent to בפנים, Num 12:14; <reference osisRef="Deut.25.9">Deu 25:9</reference> (to spit in the face). In consequence of this deep debasement of the object of scorn and spitting, the brightness and vision of his eye (sense of sight) are become dim (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.6.8">Psa 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.10">Psa 31:10</reference>) מכּעשׂ (always written with שׂ, not ס, in the book of Job), from grief, and his frames, i.e., bodily frame = members (Jer. <hi type="italic">membra</hi>, Targ. incorrectly: features), are become like a shadow all of them, as fleshless and powerless as a shadow, which is only appearance without substance. His suffering, his miserable form (זאת), is of such a kind that the upright are astonished (שׁמם, to become desolate, silent), and the guiltless (like himself and other innocent sufferers) become excited (here with vexation as in <reference osisRef="Ps.37.1">Psa 37:1</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Job.31.29">Job 31:29</reference> with joy) over the godless (who is none the less prosperous); but the righteous holds firm (without allowing himself to be disconcerted by this anomalous condition of things, though impenetrably mysterious) on his way (the way of good to which he has pledged himself), and the pure of hands (וּטהר־ as <reference osisRef="Prov.22.11">Pro 22:11</reference>, according to another mode of writing וּטהר־ with <hi type="italic">Chateph-Kametz</hi> under the ט and <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> under the ו; comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.54.9">Isa 54:9</reference>, where the form of writing וּמגּער־ <hi type="italic">umiggoor</hi> is well authorized) increases (יוסיף, of inward increase, as <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.18">Ecc 1:18</reference>) in strength (אמץ only here in the book of Job); i.e., far from allowing suffering to draw him from God to the side of the godless, he gathers strength thereby only still more perseveringly to pursue righteousness of life and purity of conduct, since suffering, especially in connection with such experiences as Job now has with the three friends, drives him to God and makes his communion with Him closer and firmer. These words of Job (if we may be allowed the figure) are like a rocket which shoots above the tragic darkness of the book, lighting it up suddenly, although only for a short time. The confession which breaks through in lyric form in Ps 73 here finds expression of a more brief, sententious kind. The point of Eliphaz' reproach (<reference osisRef="Job.15.4">Job 15:4</reference>), that Job makes void the fear of God, and depreciates communion with God, is destroyed by this confession, and the assurance of Satan (<reference osisRef="Job.2.5">Job 2:5</reference>) is confronted by a fact of experience, which, if it should also become manifest in the case of Job, puts to shame and makes void the hope of the evil spirit.
entries.e2729fae13fe6b1d95dd95a1f5e39c49483909c5: <reference osisRef="Job.17.10-Job.12.10">Job 17:10-12 10</reference>  But only come again all of you! <div eID="gen7575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7576" type="x-p"/> I shall not find a wise man among you. - 11  My days are past, My purposes cut off, <div eID="gen7576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7577" type="x-p"/> The cherished thoughts of my heart, - 12  Ye explain night as day, <div eID="gen7577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7578" type="x-p"/> Light is near when darkness sets in. <div eID="gen7578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7579" type="x-p"/> The truly righteous man, even if in the midst of his affliction he should see destruction before him, does not however forsake God. But (nevertheless) ye - he exclaims to the friends, who promise him a long and prosperous life if he will only humble himself as a sinner who is receiving punishment - repeat again and again your hortatory words on penitence! a wise man who might be able to see into my real condition, I shall not find among you. He means that they deceive themselves concerning the actual state of the case before them; for in reality he is meeting death without being deceived, or allowing himself to be deceived, about the matter. His appeal is similar to Job 6:29. Carey translates correctly: Attack me again with another round of arguments, etc. Instead of ואוּלם, as it is written everywhere else (generally when the speech is drawing to a close), we find ואלּם (as the form of writing אלם, אלּם occurs also in the subst. אוּלם), perh. in order to harmonize with כּלּם, which is here according to rule instead of כּלּכם, which corresponds more to our form of a vocative clause, just as in 1Ki 22:28; Mic 1:2 (Ewald, §327, <hi type="italic">a</hi>).<note placement="foot">Comp. my <hi type="italic">Anekdota zur Gesch. der mittelalterlichen Scholastik unter Juden und Moslemen</hi> (1841), S. 380.</note> <div eID="gen7579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7580" type="x-p"/> In וּבאוּ תּשׁוּבוּ the jussive and imper. (for the <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> יבאי, which occurs in some Codd. and editions, is meaningless) are united, the former being occasioned by the arrangement of the words, which is unfavourable to the imper. (comp. Ew. §229); moreover, the first verb gives the adverbial notion <hi type="italic">iterum, denuo</hi> to the second, according to Ges. §142, 3, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. <div eID="gen7580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7581" type="x-p"/> What follows, <reference osisRef="Job.17.11">Job 17:11</reference>, is the confirmation of the fact that there is no wise man among them who might be able to give him efficient solace by a right estimate of the magnitude and undeservedness of his suffering. His life is indeed run out; and the most cherished plans and hopes which he had hedged in and fostered for the future in his heart, he has utterly and long since given up. The <hi type="italic">plur.</hi> (occurring only here) of זמּה, which occurs also <hi type="italic">sensu malo,</hi> signifies projects, as מזמות, <reference osisRef="Job.21.27">Job 21:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.42.2">Job 42:2</reference>, from זמם, to tie; Aben-Ezra refers to the Arab. <hi type="italic">zamâm</hi> (a thread, band, esp. a rein). These plans which are now become useless, these cherished thoughts, he calls מורשׁי, <hi type="italic">peculia</hi> (from ירשׁ, to take possession of) of his heart. Thus, after Obad. Oba 1:17, Gecatilia (in Aben-Ezra) also explains, while, according to Ewald, <hi type="italic">Beiträge,</hi> S. 98, he understands the heart-strings, i.e., the trunks of the arteries (for thus is Arab. <hi type="italic">nî't</hi> to be explained), and consequently, as Ewald himself, and even Farisol, most improbably combines מורשׁ with מותר (יתר). Similarly the lxx τὰ ἄρθρα τῆς καρδίας, as though the joints (instead of the valves) of the heart were intended; probably with Middeldorpf, after the Syriac Hexapla, ἄκρα is to be read instead of ἄρθρα; this, however, rests upon a mistaking of מורשׁי for ראשׁי. While he is now almost dead, and his life-plans of the future are torn away (נתּקוּ), the friends turn night into day (שׂים, as <reference osisRef="Isa.5.20">Isa 5:20</reference>); light is (i.e., according to their opinion) nearer than the face of darkness, i.e., than the darkness which is in reality turned to him, and which is as though it stared at him from the immediate future. Thus Nolde explains it as comparative, but connecting <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.17.12">Job 17:12</reference></hi> with ישׂימו, and considering פני (which is impossible by this compar. rendering) as meaningless: <hi type="italic">lucem magis propinquam quam tenebras.</hi> It is however possible that מפני is used the same as in <reference osisRef="Job.23.17">Job 23:17</reference> : light is, as they think near before darkness, i.e., while darkness sets in (<hi type="italic">ingruentibus tenebris</hi>), according to which we have translated.
